report:
**Conclusion:** *Possibly, but the evidence is not strong enough to treat olive-leaf extract as a proven substitute for blood-pressure medication.* Small human trials suggest a modest BP-lowering effect, particularly in people with borderline or stage-1 hypertension.

A double-blind active-comparator trial in stage-1 hypertension found that 500 mg olive-leaf extract twice daily for eight weeks lowered BP, with results broadly similar to captopril. However, it did not include a placebo group, so it cannot fully separate the extract’s effect from regression to the mean or other trial effects.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/

A more rigorous randomized, double-blind crossover trial of a phenolic-rich extract also reported favorable BP findings, but it was relatively small and short-term. Extract formulations and doses differ substantially across studies, making it difficult to estimate a reliable real-world effect or select a dose.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486627/

The evidence against a confident “yes” is therefore limited study size, short duration, heterogeneous products, and lack of evidence that olive leaf prevents heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, or safely replaces standard treatment. A recent review likewise identifies evidence gaps despite promising cardiometabolic findings.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8035902/

**Practical advice:** Do not stop or reduce prescribed antihypertensives. Olive leaf may add to the effects of BP-lowering drugs and potentially cause excessively low BP; discuss it with a clinician or pharmacist—especially if taking BP or diabetes medicines, or if pregnant/breastfeeding.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/herb-drug-interactions
